story.headline: Spain stages first general strike in 14 years
story.summary: Spain's unions held a 24-hour general strike over housing and purchasing power before the 29 November snap election.
story.display_body: Spain began its first general strike in 14 years at midnight on Wednesday 11 November, a 24-hour walkout over housing costs and purchasing power less than three weeks before the snap election of Sunday 29 November. The two main unions, UGT and CCOO, reported stoppages of around 90% in the car and port sectors in the first hours, according to their own statement relayed by Al Jazeera. Public transport was disrupted, burning-tyre roadblocks went up in Barcelona, and picketers scuffled with police outside Mercamadrid, the capital's main wholesale market. Average rents in Spain have nearly doubled in ten years. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the election after his minority government failed to pass a housing package. He says the strike is "not against anyone"; business groups call it an election protest, and the conservative Popular Party and Vox have criticised it.
story.why: housing is now the central issue of an election that Al Jazeera says could bring the far right to power, and the strike measures how much pressure the unions can still apply.

story.headline: House Republicans shelve Hegseth impeachment
story.summary: The US House voted 211-204 to refer Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution to committee, effectively killing it.
story.display_body: The US House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday 10 November to send Thomas Massie's impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-led Judiciary Committee, which in practice ends the effort in this Congress. Massie, a Republican, had warned that referral would kill the resolution, which accuses Hegseth of waging the Iran war without congressional authorisation. Hegseth called the accusations "slander" and "a farce" at his first Pentagon press conference in months; Donald Trump said the effort had "miserably FAILED". Massie said his colleagues "know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board". Democrats take control of both chambers in January, and a new attempt is expected then.

story.headline: US soldier held in UK on Russia spying suspicion
story.summary: UK counter-terrorism police arrested a US Army member near Gloucester on suspicion of spying for Russia.
story.display_body: British counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old member of the US Army near Gloucester on Tuesday 10 November on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act 2023, in a case the Metropolitan Police say relates to Russia. Officers searched two locations in Gloucestershire. The Met says the investigation was run with US authorities, the US military and the FBI. FBI Director Kash Patel called the espionage allegations of "utmost concern", and the head of US Army Counterintelligence Command described the suspect as a "senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information". The area is home to Britain's signals-intelligence agency GCHQ in nearby Cheltenham and to a NATO rapid-reaction corps headquarters. The man has not been charged.

story.headline: US indicts three over Iran-linked attack plots
story.summary: An updated Manhattan indictment charges three men with plotting nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities and RAF Fairford.
story.display_body: US prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed an updated indictment on Tuesday 10 November charging three men with plotting nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the US, and on RAF Fairford, a British airbase the US used for strikes on Iran. The defendants are an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, an Iranian and an Iraqi; only the dual national, whom prosecutors describe as a commander of the Iraqi armed group Kata'ib Hizballah, is in custody. Prosecutors say he used coded calls from a US jail to arrange payments to attackers and coordinated with the others in the days before a "major incident" at Fairford in late September. He pleaded not guilty in June. The indictment ties the plots to Iran's Revolutionary Guards; Tehran has denied involvement. The US Attorney's Office's own release could not be fetched.

story.headline: Algeria jails Kamel Daoud in absentia
story.summary: An Oran court sentenced writer Kamel Daoud in absentia to five years over his novel Houris.
story.display_body: A court in Oran sentenced the French-Algerian writer Kamel Daoud in absentia to five years in prison on Tuesday 10 November for invasion of privacy and disclosure of professional secrets over his Goncourt-winning novel "Houris". The complainant, Saâda Arbane, a survivor of the 1990s civil war, says the novel used her story, which reached Daoud through his wife, the psychiatrist Aïcha Dahdouh, who was her doctor. Dahdouh was also convicted; she denies passing on the file and has started divorce proceedings. Daoud calls the verdict the result of years of "violent defamation campaigns" and frames the case as a trial of free expression.
story.why: the sentence lands as France campaigns for another of its nationals jailed in Algeria, the journalist Christophe Gleizes, and will strain relations further.

story.headline: Bern approves TARDOC revision, warns on costs
story.summary: The Federal Council approved the first TARDOC outpatient tariff revision from 2027 but demanded cost neutrality and better pay for primary care.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 11 November approved the first annual revision of the outpatient tariff system (TARDOC and outpatient flat rates) in force since January, but refused some changes and warned doctors, hospitals and insurers that it is preparing to step in on costs. The new tariffs take effect on 1 January 2027 and mainly change paediatrics, hospital emergency services, pathology and several surgical fields. The government has capped the annual rise in total outpatient costs at 4%. It says the tariff partners (FMH, H+ and prio.swiss) have still not submitted a joint plan to keep within that cap "despite repeated requests", so it has told the Interior Department to prepare measures for when the cap is exceeded. It also says the promised upgrade of primary care is not happening: on the partners' own simulations, no primary-care category gains except psychiatry and general practitioners. It wants a binding roadmap with the next request.
story.why: TARDOC replaced TARMED partly to shift money towards family doctors and paediatricians, and the government is now saying in writing that, so far, it has not.

story.headline: Federal Council rejects solar-roof initiative
story.summary: The Federal Council recommends Parliament reject the solar initiative without a counter-proposal.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 11 November recommended that Parliament reject the "solar initiative", which would require suitable roofs, walls, car parks and other structures to carry solar panels, without a counter-proposal. The initiative was filed on 10 December 2025. The government argues that the law already sets ambitious solar targets with large subsidies, and that an obligation would infringe property rights. It says buildings are mainly a cantonal matter. It also argues that a solar push large enough to cover winter demand would produce big summer surpluses and extra grid costs, and it doubts there are enough installers. It says it prefers a mix of hydro, solar, wind, biomass and nuclear. Note the contrast with today's Climate Change Performance Index (below), whose experts list the absence of solar standards for all buildings as a Swiss gap.

story.headline: Status S holders keep free travel
story.summary: The Federal Council sent Parliament a bill keeping permit-free travel abroad for Ukrainians with status S.
story.display_body: Ukrainians with protection status S will keep the right to travel abroad and return without a travel permit, under a bill the Federal Council sent to Parliament on Wednesday 11 November; asylum seekers and provisionally admitted people will face restrictions. Parliament voted in December 2021 to allow such trips only in exceptional cases, but the government never brought those rules into force, because it let Ukrainian refugees travel freely when status S was activated in March 2022. The bill writes that exception into law; it will take effect together with the 2021 rules and lapse when status S is lifted. Stays in Ukraine itself remain limited to 15 days per half-year. Most consultation responses supported keeping the exception.

story.headline: Climate index sees Switzerland missing 2030 goal
story.summary: Switzerland rose to 24th in the CCPI 2027 but experts expect it to miss its 2030 emissions target.
story.display_body: Switzerland rose two places to 24th in the Climate Change Performance Index 2027, presented on Wednesday 11 November at the COP31 climate talks, but the index's experts expect it to miss its 2030 target of halving greenhouse-gas emissions. The index, published by Germanwatch and the NewClimate Institute, rates 64 countries plus the EU on emissions, renewables, energy use and policy. It again leaves the top three places empty because no country is doing enough to meet the Paris goals. Switzerland scores relatively well on emissions and energy use, but its experts criticise thin domestic measures, funding cuts to climate programmes and heavy reliance on offsets bought abroad. They doubt Switzerland can buy enough credits that meet its own legal requirements. They also flag slow electric-car uptake, slow phase-out of gas heating and the country's role as a hub for commodity traders. Switzerland ranks behind France (20th) and ahead of Germany (25th), Austria (33rd) and Italy (41st).

story.headline: Italian top court quashes Schmidheiny conviction
story.summary: Italy's Court of Cassation quashed Stephan Schmidheiny's Eternit asbestos sentence and sent part of the case back to Turin.
story.display_body: Italy's Court of Cassation on the evening of Tuesday 10 November quashed the nine-and-a-half-year sentence handed to Swiss former industrialist Stephan Schmidheiny for negligent homicide in 91 asbestos deaths linked to the Eternit plant at Casale Monferrato. The court ruled that 25 of the deaths are time-barred and sent the remaining roughly 60 back to Turin for a new trial. Schmidheiny, now 79, headed the Swiss Eternit group from 1976 to 1986. His defence argued that personal causation for each victim's illness had not been proven; the court's written reasons are due in a few weeks. No conviction against Schmidheiny has yet survived Italy's top court. Victims' relatives at the hearing called it "a real injustice" and warned that more cases will lapse.

story.headline: Unions push 5,000-franc wage for apprentices
story.summary: The Swiss Trade Union Federation plans an initiative for a 5,000-franc minimum wage for VET certificate holders.
story.display_body: The Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB/USS) wants a popular initiative guaranteeing a minimum wage of CHF 5,000 a month for anyone who has completed an apprenticeship, Le Temps reported on Wednesday 11 November. The federation says 28% of holders of a federal VET certificate (CFC/EFZ, the standard apprenticeship diploma) earn less than CHF 5,000 gross, and that their inflation-adjusted median wage has fallen 2.1% since 2016. Its congress decides at the end of this week; if approved, signature collection would start next year. The employers' association opposes it, saying vocational training's strength is access and mobility in the labour market, not a state-guaranteed starting wage. A poll commissioned by the unions found 66% in favour.

story.headline: Atoms cooled below 10 picokelvin in orbit
story.summary: A Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) is a cloud of atoms cooled so far that they share one quantum state and behave like a single wave.
story.display_body: A Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) is a cloud of atoms cooled so far that they share one quantum state and behave like a single wave. In space you can let the cloud float and expand for seconds without it falling, and slower expansion means a lower "equivalent temperature". The previous record, 38 picokelvin (trillionths of a degree above absolute zero) with 2 s of free expansion, used magnetic traps on an atom chip. This team made the condensate aboard the China Space Station in an optical dipole trap, which holds atoms with focused laser light rather than magnetic fields. That design has better optical access and can also trap non-magnetic atoms, but no one had used it to make a quantum gas in microgravity before. Their cloud of 2.0 × 10⁴ atoms reached 9.7 pK (+3.2/−2.7) and expanded freely for 7.0 s. The result rests on the paper's own measurement. Science's news section calls it the coldest temperature yet produced, but no independent group has checked it.
story.why: longer, colder free fall is what atom interferometers need for tests of gravity and the equivalence principle in space. It also shows that laser-based traps, which suit more atomic species, now work in orbit.
affiliations: Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics

story.headline: Cuprate pseudogap marks where electrons pair
story.summary: In copper-oxide ("cuprate") high-temperature superconductors, a partial energy gap called the pseudogap opens well above the temperature at which the material superconducts.
story.display_body: In copper-oxide ("cuprate") high-temperature superconductors, a partial energy gap called the pseudogap opens well above the temperature at which the material superconducts. For three decades one camp has said it shows electrons already pairing up without yet moving in step. The other camp says it is a competing order, such as charge-density waves (periodic ripples in electron density). The Leiden-led team used local shot-noise spectroscopy on Bi₂Sr₂CaCu₂O₈₊δ. Shot noise is the graininess of an electric current, and it doubles when charge moves in pairs (2e) rather than as single electrons. They find that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of pairing, that it varies from place to place, and that it reaches up to 70 meV. The authors say this rules out an origin purely in local order. In their reading, cuprates are limited by phase coherence (getting the pairs to lock in step), not by forming pairs at all.
story.why: if pairs already exist at the pseudogap scale, the way to raise the superconducting temperature is to make those pairs coherent, not to make new ones. That narrows a debate that has shaped materials research for 30 years. The work comes from Dutch and German labs.

story.headline: Iron melts lower at core pressures
story.summary: The temperature of Earth's core is set by where iron melts at enormous pressure, and estimates have disagreed by more than 1,000 K.
story.display_body: The temperature of Earth's core is set by where iron melts at enormous pressure, and estimates have disagreed by more than 1,000 K. Carnegie's team squeezed iron in diamond anvil cells and heated it with microsecond current pulses (pulsed Joule heating), spotting melting as a brief temperature plateau. The plateau marks the latent heat being absorbed. More than 300 reproducible runs give a surprisingly shallow melting curve, rising about 6 K per gigapascal and reaching 4,160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. The team also measured liquid iron's electrical resistivity, 76 μΩ·cm. Extrapolating to core pressures and alloy composition, they infer a relatively cold core–mantle boundary of about 3,430 K and a low heat flow from the outer core of about 9.8 TW. The extrapolation is the uncertain step, and these numbers are the authors' model inference, not direct measurements of the core.
story.why: a cooler core with lower resistivity means ordinary thermal convection could have powered Earth's magnetic field before the solid inner core formed. That bears on the long-running "new core paradox" about how the early magnetic field was sustained. It also implies that the lowest mantle is fully solid today.

story.headline: Ice-age ocean flips took over a century
story.summary: During the last ice age, Greenland repeatedly warmed by many degrees in "Dansgaard–Oeschger" (DO) events.
story.display_body: During the last ice age, Greenland repeatedly warmed by many degrees in "Dansgaard–Oeschger" (DO) events. These are usually read as abrupt restarts of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), the current system that carries heat north toward Europe. Greenland ice cores suggest each warming took only decades, or about ten years. This team used precisely dated cave formations (speleothems) from the Asian monsoon region, whose oxygen isotopes track the same events. Those records show the warmings unfolding over more than a century. Isotope modelling reconciles the two archives. Greenland mostly records a fast change in atmospheric circulation, triggered when sea ice first retreated in the northeastern North Atlantic. The ocean overturning and the hemisphere's heat balance adjusted much more slowly.
story.why: "abrupt" ice-core transitions are often used as benchmarks for how fast the AMOC can switch. This paper says those benchmarks measure the atmosphere's response, not the ocean's. Europe's climate depends on the AMOC, so the distinction matters, although the paper is about natural glacial events, not today's warming.

story.headline: 3.95-billion-year-old rock found in China
story.summary: Rocks older than 3.9 billion years are so rare that the only accepted examples come from the Acasta Gneiss in Canada.
story.display_body: Rocks older than 3.9 billion years are so rare that the only accepted examples come from the Acasta Gneiss in Canada. This team reports a 3.95-billion-year-old trondhjemitic gneiss, a light-coloured granite-like rock, from eastern Hebei in the North China Craton. Zircon crystals in it have elevated oxygen-18 (δ¹⁸O about +6.8‰) and positive hafnium-isotope values. Together these suggest the magma came from basalt that had been altered by water near the surface, itself derived from a mantle already depleted during the Hadean, Earth's first eon. Thermodynamic modelling puts its formation at more than 1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, by low-degree melting of basaltic crust. That requires surface rock to have been buried quickly to mantle depths along a cool path. The authors propose a "transient subduction event", one plate sinking beneath another, rather than continuous plate tectonics. Nature's news coverage treats it as a second window on the period alongside Acasta.
story.why: when plate tectonics began is one of geology's biggest open questions, and a second >3.9-billion-year-old rock body with a high-pressure signature gives that debate a new data point. One sample site is a narrow base, and "transient subduction" is the authors' interpretation.

story.headline: Stopping statins after 70 passes, with a cost
story.summary: Statins clearly prevent heart attacks in middle-aged people, but whether people over 70 who never had cardiovascular disease should keep taking them has never been tested in a randomised trial.
story.display_body: Statins clearly prevent heart attacks in middle-aged people, but whether people over 70 who never had cardiovascular disease should keep taking them has never been tested in a randomised trial. STREAM, sponsored by Inselspital and run mostly through Swiss hospitals and family doctors, randomised 1,880 people aged 70 or older to stop or continue their statin. Sites were in Switzerland, the Netherlands and France, and every participant had at least two chronic conditions. Mean age was 77.5. The main test was non-inferiority: was stopping not meaningfully worse over two years? It passed. Event-free time over two years was 96.5 weeks after stopping versus 98.5 weeks with continuing. The difference of −2.0 weeks fell inside the prespecified −5.2-week margin. But over a median 103 weeks, the composite of non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal ischaemic stroke or death occurred in 12.7% of those who stopped versus 9.2% of those who continued (hazard ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.05–1.81). The investigators estimate one extra major event or death per 40 people who stop over two years. In June 2026 the safety board recommended that people in the stop arm be told to discuss restarting with their doctor. So the trial met its pre-set test while also showing measurable harm, and commentators disagree about which reading should guide practice. The NEJM full text was not reachable here, so the figures come from HCPLive's report of the paper.
story.why: this is the first real evidence on a decision that millions of older people face, and it comes from Swiss primary care. The authors' own conclusion is "cautious" discontinuation only after shared decision-making, not a general licence to stop.

story.headline: Scythian hair shows 2,800-year-old cannabis use
story.summary: A team led by Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari excavated a monumental Scythian tomb in Tuva, southern Siberia.
story.display_body: A team led by Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari excavated a monumental Scythian tomb in Tuva, southern Siberia. The Scythians were a horse-riding culture of the Eurasian steppe. The tomb held about 1,000 cannabis seeds, and radiocarbon dating of six of them places the burial in the early 8th century BC. Seeds alone do not prove anyone got high, since hemp was also grown for oil and fibre. The decisive evidence came from preserved human hair. High-resolution mass spectrometry found clear signals matching cannabinol (CBN), a breakdown product of THC, the plant's main psychoactive compound, plus weak signals consistent with THC itself. The Bern release is careful about the limits. The hair cannot say how much was consumed, or whether it was smoked or eaten. The seeds come from wild or feral plants, so they do not show cultivation.
story.why: it pushes direct, in-the-body evidence of psychoactive cannabis use back to at least 2,800 years ago. It also combines plant remains with chemistry from a human body, a method other sites can copy.

story.headline: Pill-tuned gene therapy nearly stops seizures
story.summary: The three adults had temporal-lobe epilepsy caused by scarring of one hippocampus (hippocampal sclerosis).
story.display_body: The three adults had temporal-lobe epilepsy caused by scarring of one hippocampus (hippocampal sclerosis). They had been diagnosed 10–25 years earlier and had become resistant to at least two drugs. Surgeons infused an adeno-associated virus (AAV9, a harmless virus used as a gene courier) into the patch of brain where each person's seizures start. The virus carried a gene that makes excitatory neurons produce a designer receptor that responds to clozapine. This approach is called chemogenetics. Two weeks after surgery, patients started low-dose clozapine every eight hours, which switches the receptor on and quiets the targeted neurons. Unlike conventional gene therapy, the dose can be adjusted, or stopped. About two months later, monthly seizures had fallen from 4.5 to 0.5 in two patients and from 4 to 0 in the third, with no serious side effects. This is a three-patient report, published as a correspondence letter rather than a full trial. Clozapine at high doses carries cardiovascular and other risks, and long-term use is unstudied. An outside neurologist quoted by Nature raised both points.
story.why: it is a first human proof that a brain circuit can be gene-modified and then tuned with a pill. If it holds up in larger trials, it could become an option for patients who would otherwise need part of their brain surgically removed.

story.headline: Pelacarsen cuts Lp(a) but not heart events
story.summary: Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a genetically set cholesterol-carrying particle.
story.display_body: Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), is a genetically set cholesterol-carrying particle. Genetic studies strongly link high levels to heart disease, and there is no approved drug for it. Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (a short synthetic strand that silences the gene's messenger RNA), is developed by Novartis under licence from Ionis. The trial randomised 8,350 patients with prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease and Lp(a) of at least 70 mg/dL to monthly injections or placebo. The topline miss was announced in September. The full data show how flat the result was. Lp(a) fell 78.4% at 12 months, yet over a median 4.7 years the primary composite (cardiovascular death, heart attack, stroke or urgent revascularisation) occurred in 12.3% versus 12.1% (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.90–1.15). The result was the same in patients with the highest Lp(a). Flu-like and injection-site reactions were far more common on the drug, 20.6% versus 7.5% stopped treatment because of side effects, and 19 patients on pelacarsen had adjudicated anaphylaxis versus none on placebo.
story.why: it is a sharp reminder that lowering a risk marker does not guarantee fewer events. It is a major setback for Basel-based Novartis's cardiovascular pipeline, and the question now passes to other Lp(a) drugs still in outcome trials.

story.headline: Earliest close quasar pair found at cosmic dawn
story.summary: A quasar is a supermassive black hole feeding so fast that it outshines its whole galaxy.
story.display_body: A quasar is a supermassive black hole feeding so fast that it outshines its whole galaxy. When galaxies merge, their quasars should sometimes appear in close pairs, but such pairs are short-lived, faint and hard to separate at great distances. Using Gemini North and JWST, the team found J1602+4228AB, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua by a Hawaiian-language naming programme. It is a pair of quasars about 18,100 light-years apart, roughly a fifth of the Milky Way's diameter, seen when the Universe was about 900 million years old. That makes it the most distant and most compact quasar pair known from "cosmic dawn", and only the third pair found from that era. The black holes weigh about 1.5 billion and 400 million solar masses. Lead author Silvia Onorato says there is no definitive theoretical explanation for how even one such giant existed so early, "much less two". It is a single system, so it shows such objects exist but does not say how common they are.
story.why: it adds to the JWST-era evidence that black holes grew faster in the young Universe than standard models allow, and it catches two of them on course for a merger. European groups at INAF and Heidelberg are core members of the survey.

story.headline: Rocky exoplanets shed volatiles like Earth
story.summary: Earlier studies found that rocky exoplanets carry more iron relative to silicon than their host stars.
story.display_body: Earlier studies found that rocky exoplanets carry more iron relative to silicon than their host stars. That was usually explained by planets somehow collecting extra iron. Earth shows a different pattern called devolatilization. Compared with the Sun, it is depleted in volatile elements such as oxygen and sulfur but keeps refractory ones such as iron and magnesium, which survive heat. The team revisited 14 rocky planets of 0.5–10 Earth masses whose stars have measured iron, silicon, magnesium, oxygen and sulfur abundances. They inferred each planet's interior from its mass and radius using two independent models. Eight of the 14 follow an Earth-like devolatilization trend, and only one matches its star one-to-one. The two models agree. The authors name the limits: a sample of 14, few planets with good stellar chemistry, and little range in orbital distance. They expect ESA's PLATO mission to extend the sample.
story.why: it suggests that the processes that shaped Earth's composition may be common, which makes "Earth-like" a more natural outcome of planet formation than a fluke.
